blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — prenatal opioid exposure and neonatal withdrawal
stem: A newborn with prenatal opioid exposure is being monitored for neonatal withdrawal. Which finding is most consistent with neonatal abstinence syndrome/neonatal opioid withdrawal?

options.A: Tremors, irritability or excessive high-pitched crying, and poor feeding or sucking are recognized withdrawal findings after prenatal opioid exposure.
options.B: Persistent flaccidity without irritability, tremors, feeding difficulty, or autonomic signs is the characteristic withdrawal pattern after prenatal opioid exposure.
options.C: Isolated jaundice without neurologic, feeding, gastrointestinal, or autonomic findings is the expected presentation of opioid withdrawal in newborns.
options.D: Prenatal opioid exposure cannot produce neonatal withdrawal symptoms, so tremors, irritability, or poor feeding should be attributed to another cause.

rationale: CDC states that neonatal abstinence syndrome can occur when newborns withdraw from substances, including opioids, that they were exposed to before birth. Current CDC guidance lists tremors, irritability or excessive/high-pitched crying, hyperactive reflexes, and poor feeding or sucking among possible withdrawal signs. CDC also notes that not every opioid-exposed newborn develops NAS and severity varies. Therefore A is correct. B and C do not reflect the characteristic withdrawal pattern, and D incorrectly denies that prenatal opioid exposure can cause neonatal withdrawal.
educational_objective: Recognize tremors, irritability or high-pitched crying, and poor feeding or sucking as common neonatal withdrawal findings after prenatal opioid exposure, while recognizing that not every exposed newborn develops NAS/NOWS.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_locator: Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS), lines 73-85: opioid use during pregnancy can lead to NAS in some newborns; withdrawal signs may include tremors, irritability/excessive or high-pitched crying, hyperactive reflexes, and poor feeding/sucking.
source_claim_supported: Prenatal opioid exposure can lead to NAS/NOWS in some newborns; possible signs include tremors, irritability or high-pitched crying, and poor feeding or sucking, with variable severity.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12/PDF p.16: monitor for medication/substance effects and adverse reactions; provide safe medication-related care.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices as complete neonatal-withdrawal presentations without absolute-word distractor cues.
Used current May 2026 CDC language and explicitly preserved variability in whether NAS occurs and how severe it is.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A uniquely matches current CDC withdrawal signs. B and C describe noncharacteristic patterns, D contradicts CDC, and the stem does not imply that every opioid-exposed newborn develops withdrawal.
